title: Chapter XLVI

teacherSummary.text: Letters from Jane report that Lydia has run off with Wickham, possibly not married. Darcy finds Elizabeth distraught; she confides in him. Elizabeth and the Gardiners hurry home.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLVI,” how does Austen show scandal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLVI develops the idea of scandal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XLVI to complicate the reader's understanding of scandal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of scandal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of scandal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why does Elizabeth tell Darcy, and what does she fear? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include fluctuating, actuated, superseded, informing, darting. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Her affections had been continually fluctuating, but never without an object.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To move as a wave.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. An unmarried elopement could ruin the reputation of an entire family. Now, why does this chapter matter? The crisis tests Darcy's love and reveals Elizabeth's change of heart. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Conflict, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot plot, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
